title: Dynamic tests (stimulation & suppression)
html:
Source: Dynamic tests.pdf – 4 pages

PITUITARY GLAND #1

  • Hypopituitarism Stimulation tests
  • For GH and ACTH secretory reserve
  • Insulin tolerance test (ITT)
  • - Regular insulin is given IV in a dose of 0.1-0,15 IU/kg (“healthy” individuals)/ 0.2-0.3
  • IU/kg (obese patients/ patients with Cushing)
  • - Blood glucose level <40 mg/dl at 15 min + signs and symptoms of hypoglycaemia are
  • necessary for adequate stimulation
  • - Blood samples of GH +/- cortisol are obtained at 0, 30, 45, 60, 75, and 90 min
  • - Side effects: severe hypoglycaemia (in which case 20-40 ml of 33% glucose are given
  • IV)
  • - Normal response: GH should increase to a maximal level >7 ng/ml (children)/ >3 ng/ml
  • (adults)
  • Cortisol should increase to a peak level of at least 18-20 μg/dl
  • - No response or subnormal response = GH / ACTH deficiency
  • - After the test is finished, the patient should receive a meal with high glycaemic content
  • Other tests for GH reserve
  • Clonidine test:
  • - Clonidine is given orally in a dose of 0,15 mg/m2
  • - Blood samples of GH are obtained at 0, 30, 60, 90, 120 and 150 min
  • - Side effects: hypotension- during the test the BP should be monitored
  • - Normal response: GH will increase >7 ng/ml (children)/ >3 ng/ml (adults)
  • - No response or subnormal response = GH deficiency
  • For LH and FSH secretory reserves
  • GnRH (gonadorelin) test:
  • - GnRH is given IV in a dose of 100 µg
  • - Blood samples for LH and FSH are obtained at 0, 30 and 60 min
  • - Normal response: LH increases 4–5 times over the basal levels/ an increase in the LH
  • level of 1.3–2.6 g/l (12–23 IU/l); FSH usually responds more slowly and less markedly
  • - No response or subnormal response = FSH/LH deficiency
  • For TSH secretory reserve
  • TRH test:
  • - TRH is given IV in a dose of 200 µg- 400 µg
  • - Blood samples of TSH (+/- PRL) are obtained at 0, 30 and 60 min
  • - Side effects: nausea, metallic taste
  • - Normal response: TSH level increases 2 times over the basal levels at 60 min
  • - No response or subnormal response = TSH deficiency
  • !! Nowadays its main use is in the differential diagnosis of elevated TSH in the setting
  • of elevated thyroid hormone levels resistance to thyroid hormone vs a TSH-secreting
  • pituitary adenoma.
  • For ACTH secretory reserve
  • ⇒
  • CRH test:
  • - CRH is given IV in a dose of 100 µg
  • - Blood samples of ACTH+ cortisol are obtained at 0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90 and 120 min
  • - Normal response: -ACTH increases 2 times over the basal levels
  • - plasma cortisol should increase to a peak level of at least 18–20 μg/dl
  • - No response or subnormal response = ACTH deficiency

Short Synacthen test (Rapid ACTH stimulation test): #2

  • - Synthetic ACTH (1–24) (cosyntropin/ Synachten) is given IV/IM in a dose of 250 μg
  • - Blood samples of plasma cortisol are obtained at 0, 30, and 60 min
  • - Side effects: anaphylactic shock, nausea, vomiting, palpitations
  • - Normal response: peak plasma cortisol level >18–20 μg/dl
  • !! Note that falsely normal results occur when hypopituitarism is of recent onset because
  • the test relies on the fact that ACTH deficiency causes atrophy of the adrenal cortex and,
  • therefore, a delayed response to Synacthen
  • Acromegaly Inhibition tests
  • Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT):
  • - Proves the autonomous secretion of GH
  • - 75 g of glucose dissolved in a glass of cold water are given orally, over the course of 5 min
  • - Side effects: nausea
  • - Blood samples of GH and glycemia are obtained at 0’, 30’, 60’ and 120’
  • - Normal response: GH at 60’ <0.4 ng/ml
  • !! If the patient has diabetes mellitus the 24 h GH mean is used instead (normal response:
  • 24h GH mean< 1 ng/ml)

ADRENAL GLANDS #3

  • Addison Stimulating tests
  • Rapid ACTH stimulation test
  • - measures the acute adrenal response to ACTH and is used to diagnose both primary (PAI)
  • and secondary adrenal insufficiency (SAI).
  • - 250 µg ACTH 1-24 (SynacthenR, Cortrosyn) are given IV/IM. Blood samples of
  • plasma cortisol are obtained at 0, 30, and 60 min.
  • - Side effects: anaphylactic shock, nausea, vomiting, palpitations
  • - Normal response: peak plasma cortisol level >18–20 μg/dl (550 nmol/l)- excludes both
  • primary adrenal insufficiency (by directly assessing adrenal reserve) and overt secondary
  • adrenal insufficiency with adrenal atrophy.
  • !! However, a normal response does not rule out recently developed SAI (in which case
  • the adrenal glands might not have undergone atrophy yet) and partial ACTH deficiency
  • (decreased pituitary reserve) in patients whose basal ACTH secretion is sufficient to
  • prevent adrenocortical atrophy. These patients may be unable to further increase ACTH
  • secretion and thus may have subnormal pituitary ACTH responsiveness to stress or
  • hypoglycaemia. In such patients, further testing with induced hypoglycaemia (ITT)
  • may be indicated.
  • - PAI – an ACTH stimulated peak serum cortisol <500 nmol/l (absent response)
  • - SAI – absent response initially; the normal response appears after 3-4 days of ⊕ with
  • ACTH
  • Cushing Inhibition tests
  • Small inhibition (2 possibilities):
  •  1-mg overnight dexamethasone (DXM) test (Bricaire test; 1 mg DST)
  • - Blood samples of plasma cortisol are obtained in the morning, a jeun (basal/ 8:00 cortisol)
  • and 1 mg of DXM is administered in the evening at 23:00. Blood samples of plasma
  • cortisol are obtained again the following morning at 8:00.
  • - Normal response: cortisol after 1 mg DXM< 50 nmol/l (< 18 ng/ml/ 1,8 μg/dl)
  •  Liddle 2x2 (Longer low-dose DST (2 mg/day for 48 h) (LDDST)= the optimal
  • test for those with psychiatric problems, morbid obesity, alcoholism- it allows
  • for the differential diagnosis between Cushing and pseudoCushing
  • - Blood samples of plasma cortisol are obtained in the morning, a jeun (basal/ 8:00 cortisol)
  • and DXM is administered in a dose of 2 mg/day for two days (0.5 mg every 6 hours).
  • Blood samples of plasma cortisol are obtained on the third day in the morning at 8:00.
  • - Normal response: cortisol after LDDST< 50 nmol/l (< 18 ng/ml/ 1,8 μg/dl)
  • Great inhibition (2 possibilities):
  •  8 mg (high dose) overnight dexamethasone test
  • – Blood samples of plasma cortisol are obtained in the morning, a jeun (basal/ 8:00
  • cortisol) and 8 mg of DXM are administered in the evening at 23:00. Blood samples of
  • plasma cortisol are obtained again the following morning at 8:00.
  • - Normal response: cortisol after 8 mg DXM ↓ with> 50% vs. basal
  •  Liddle 2x8:
  • - Blood samples of plasma cortisol are obtained in the morning, a jeun (basal/ 8:00 cortisol)
  • and DXM is administered in a dose of 8 mg/day for two days (2 mg every 6 hours). Blood

samples of plasma cortisol are obtained on the third day in the morning at 8:00. #4

  • - Normal response: cortisol after 8 mg DXM ↓ with> 50% vs. basal
  • - in Cushing’s disease- normal response
  • - in paraneoplastic Cushing and in ACTH-independent forms- cortisol after 8 mg DXM
  • fails to decrease with> 50% vs. basal
  • Pseudo-Cushing (functional hypersecretion of de CRH - normal response (suppression)
  • in patients with psychiatric problems, morbid obesity, for the small inhibition test
  • alcoholism etc.)
  • Cushing disease - no suppression for the small
  • inhibition test
  • - normal response (suppression)
  • for the great inhibition test
  • Paraneoplastic Cushing and ACTH independent - no suppression for both small
  • forms (adenoma, adenocarcinoma, hyperplasia) inhibition tests and great
  • inhibition tests
